content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a Multiple Invertible and Equivariant transformation (MIE-transformation) VAE model for disentanglement. The general idea is to introduce inductive biases to latent spaces, and learn invertible latent-to-latent transformations. The prior and posterior in the VAE framework is learnt through approximated exponential family. The experimental results show the proposed MIET-VAE outperforms prior works like beta-VAE, beta-TCVAE and group VAE.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles the challenging task of unsupervised disentanglement - inferring the true latent factors of variation simply by observing the distribution of data. The suggested approach uses a deterministic transformation of the latent codes that is based on the matrix exponential - which is invertible. The paper claims and presents a mathematical proof that it preserves equivariance in some sense better than unrestricted matriix transformation. It then tries to relax the gaussianity assumption by an exponential family one and presents some losses terms to preserve the identity of distributions. Finally, it presents numerical results on several toy datasets with low to moderate performance gains.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Unfortunately, I found the paper hard to penetrate due to its complicated and overly mathematical presentation. It is quite possible that I missed many of its strengths (or weaknesses). 

I believe its main strength is showing that transformation by an invertible matrix preserves equivariance better than by unconstrained matrices. From reading the paper, I could not assess the significance of this results - and the authors' themselves say that the proof does not apply in many real cases. 

Another strength was the exponential family parametrization, whille it seemed significant in the ablation study - perhaps another reviewer could comment on its novelty? 

Clarity is probably the main weakness of this work. Even the method figure was more confusing than helpful. Improving this is probably the lowest hanging fruit.

The experiments were carried out on toy datasets - looking at the commonly used DCI metric, the improvement were typically not particularly significant. Also, as the latest methods from NeurIPS/ICLR were not reeported but only the oldest methods, I am not sure the results are significant.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the paper is not well written. I have published and read disentanglement papers for several years but it was hard for me to understand the core method and ideas after several readings. I expect that the paper can be much improved by giving clear intution and perhaps more examples of when and why the proposed approach is likely to work.

Quality: the experiments were carried out on toy datasets. Additionally only the classic (i.e. old) disentanglement papers were compared against. As I have seen many papers in recent conferences claiming to achieve better performance

Novelty: As this method is quite complex, it is very unlikely that a previous work with the same content has been published. But its lack of clarity makes it hard for me to understand whether there is a significant new idea that can be taken from this work.

Reproducibility: Code is provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe the main issue here is clarity, the paper is unacceptable in its current form and needs a major revision. Furthermore, comparing against more recent methods and on more difficult datasets (e.g. SmallNORB) would make the results more siignificant.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Cd5y (Part 1 of 2)
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments and suggestions.
>**Question 1.**
The paper states an abelian group (Symmetric Matrix group) action on some vector space is equivariant with respect to itself. Although this follows from the commutative property, it was argued with a couple of proposition. The main problem, however, is the argument that the equivariance extends to input-to-latent (I2L) transformation. Formally, this would mean the following is true $q(\psi_{M_i}(x))= \psi_{M_j}(q(x))$ for some $M_i, M_j \in Sym(n)$, where $Sym(n)$ denotes the Lie algebra of the symmetric matrix group, $x$ the input data, and $q(\cdot)$ the encoder. This condition is shown to be true neither for a special nor for a general case of $q(\cdot)$. However it is claimed to be true in Proposition 2. Please either clarify/correct, as this the main contributions of the paper.
 
### Answer Q1.

1. The definition of equivariant function, $q_\phi (g_I \circ x) = g_L \circ q_\phi(x)$, is introduced in [1-2],. This equivariance has been empirically shown to improve disentanglement [3-4], so we used it as the base equivariance definition considered in this paper.

2. We are not arguing that I2L-transformation is equivariant.
We argue that if an encoder is equivariant between the input and latent vector space, then our method guarantees to preserve the equivariance over a subset of its corresponding symmetries after the proposed L2L-invertible transformation. The proposition 2 implies this argument ($q_\phi (\psi (g_I^a \circ x)) = g_T^a \circ q_\phi (\psi (x))$).
The argument is proposed because our method is attachable to an encoder of various VAEs enhancing disentanglement (VAE, $\beta$-VAE, $\beta$-TCVAE, and Commutative Lie Group VAE), so the equivariance between input and latent space after applying the method is affected by whether the encoder has equivariance. 
We assume that previous works are equivariant over a subset of symmetries on the input and latent vector space, as called ‘potentially existing equivariance’, because these works have improved disentanglement learning.
In this condition, our method induces the effect to preserve their potentially existing equivariance of the encoder while obtaining the benefit of invertible L2L-transformation [5].
We clarify this point by adding details of motivation on the ‘Why Should L2L transformation Be Equivariant?’ paragraph in the 3.1 section, and by revising Figure 1, and 2. The revised contents are highlighted in the manuscript.

[1] “Group Equivariant Convolutional Networks”, Taco S. Cohen, Max Welling, ICML 2016.

[2] “On the Generalization of Equivariance and convolution in Neural Networks”, Risi Kondoe, Shubhendu Trivedi, ICML 2018.

[3] “Commutative lie group VAE for disentanglement learning”, Xinqi Zhu, Chan Xu, and Dacheng Tao, ICML 2021.

[4] “Groupifyvae: from group-based definition to vae-based unsupervised representation disentanglement”, Tao Yang, Xuanchi Ren, Yuwang Wang, Wenjun Zeng, Nannig Zhen, and Pengju Ren, ICLR 2022.

[5] “Intel-vaes: Adding inductive basis to variational auto-encoder via intermediary latents”, Ning Miao, Emile Mathieu, N. Siddharth, Yee Whye Tech, and Tom Rainforth, arXiv 2021.

---

>**Question 2.**
I have not seen a discussion on how the M's are choose for those K samples in Eq(1)? are these randomly picked if so according to what distribution?
 
### Answer Q2.
We think your question can be interpreted in two ways, so we will answer both:
1. If the reviewer means K as the number of M (MIE-transformation)
>We prove that the number of MIE-transformation is equal to $\beta$ of $\beta$-VAE in Appendix A, so we used the same values for K introduced with the model. 

2. If the reviewer means the K as the sample from Gaussian distribution 
>1. $\mathbf{z}$ is sampled from $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$. 
>2. Then the $\mathbf{z}$ fed into all M ($\psi(\cdot)$: Multiple Invertible and Equivariant Transformation).
>3. Each M generates $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$.
>4. Each M is trained for forcing $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ to be EF distribution by EF similarity loss ($\mathcal{L}_{el}$).
